A first stop before [Classic Synths Compared](synth-compare.qmd). Short sections, one idea each. Click a heading to fold or open it.

::: {.ik-do}
**What you'll do**

1. Read what the ARP 2600 is and when it was made.
2. Learn its sound, one idea at a time.
3. Take a guided tour: press each **▶ Hear step** button and listen for one change.
4. Find records it is on.
5. Check yourself with a short quiz.
:::

## What it is

- The **ARP 2600** was made by **ARP Instruments** from **1971** to 1981 (Wikipedia, "ARP 2600").
- It is **semi-modular**: its parts are already joined inside, but patch cords can join them in new ways (Wikipedia; ARP 2600 M manual, pp. 5-15).
- It was "heavily marketed to high schools and universities" (Wikipedia): it was made for learning.

## Its sound

- **Three oscillators** (VCO-1, 2 and 3) (ARP 2600 M manual, pp. 7-9).
- A **ring modulator** multiplies two waves and makes bell and metal sounds (manual, p. 14).
- **Sample and hold** grabs a random voltage on each clock tick: the classic random "bleeps" (manual, p. 15).
- Its filter falls off at 24 dB per octave (ARP 2600 owner's manual, 1971, section 4.12).

## Guided tour

Each step loads a worked example and changes one thing.

```{=html}
<div class="ik-step" data-ex="arp-ring" data-set="{&quot;inRing&quot;:0,&quot;inV3&quot;:8}"><p><b>A plain wave.</b> VCO-3's sawtooth into the filter. Listen: a simple tone.</p></div>
<div class="ik-step" data-ex="arp-ring"><p><b>The ring modulator.</b> The filter now hears the ring modulator instead. Listen for a bell: notes that do not sound quite in tune.</p></div>
<div class="ik-step" data-ex="arp-ring" data-set="{&quot;f2&quot;:12}"><p><b>Move VCO-2.</b> VCO-2 a whole octave higher feeds the ring modulator. Listen: the bell's tone changes.</p></div>
<div class="ik-step" data-ex="arp-sh" data-set="{&quot;res&quot;:0}"><p><b>Sample and hold.</b> A patch cord sends the S/H output to VCO-3's pitch. Listen for random pitches, one per clock tick.</p></div>
<div class="ik-step" data-ex="arp-sh"><p><b>Add resonance.</b> The same patch with <b>Resonance</b> at 6. Listen: each random note rings.</p></div>
<div class="ik-step" data-ex="arp-sh" data-set="{&quot;shRate&quot;:9}"><p><b>Faster clock.</b> S/H clock up to 9. Listen: the random notes come much faster.</p></div>
```

## Famous records

Named in Wikipedia, "ARP 2600":

- Genesis, *A Trick of the Tail* and *...And Then There Were Three...* (Tony Banks)
- Black Sabbath, "Who Are You?" on *Sabbath Bloody Sabbath* (Ozzy Osbourne)
- Michael Jackson, "Thriller"
- Nine Inch Nails, "The Becoming" (Flood)

```{=html}
<div class="ik-q" data-a="0"><p><b>&quot;Semi-modular&quot; means…</b></p><ul><li>Joined inside, but patch cords can change it</li><li>It has no knobs</li><li>It plays only drums</li><li>It is a computer program</li></ul><p class="ik-why">Wikipedia; manual pp. 5-15.</p></div>
<div class="ik-q" data-a="0"><p><b>Which part makes the random bleeps?</b></p><ul><li>Sample and hold</li><li>Reverb</li><li>The keyboard</li><li>The volume knob</li></ul><p class="ik-why">Steps 4-6.</p></div>
<div class="ik-q" data-a="0"><p><b>A ring modulator is good for…</b></p><ul><li>Bells and metal sounds</li><li>A clean piano</li><li>Silence</li><li>Tuning</li></ul><p class="ik-why">Step 2.</p></div>
<div class="ik-q" data-a="0"><p><b>Who was the ARP 2600 marketed to?</b></p><ul><li>High schools and universities</li><li>Only rock stars</li><li>Churches</li><li>Radio stations</li></ul><p class="ik-why">Wikipedia.</p></div>
```
